:::{#thm-hazard-dens-surv}
#### Hazard equals density over survival

If $T$ is a continuous random variable with [density](#def-pdf) $f(t)$
and [survival function](#def-surv-fn) $\surv(t)$,
then for every $t$ with $\surv(t) > 0$ at which $f$ is continuous:

$$\haz(t) = \frac{f(t)}{\surv(t)}$$

:::

::: proof

The proof uses three facts.
First, for $\change > 0$ the event $\{t \le T < t + \change\}$ is a subset of the event $\{T \ge t\}$,
so intersecting them leaves $\{t \le T < t + \change\}$
(the [subset property](probability-basics.qmd#thm-prob-subset)).
Second, $\Pr(T = t) = 0$ for a continuous $T$,
so $\Pr(T \ge t) = \Pr(T > t) = \surv(t)$, which is positive.
Third, because $f$ is continuous at $t$,
@thm-density-limit gives $f(t)$ as the limit of $\Pr(t \le T < t + \change) / \change$.

$$
\ba
\haz(t)
&\eqdef \lim_{\change \downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \change \mid T \ge t)}{\change}
&& \text{(definition of the hazard function)} \\
&= \lim_{\change \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\change} \cd \frac{\Pr(\{t \le T < t + \change\} \cap \{T \ge t\})}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \lim_{\change \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\change} \cd \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \change)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(subset property)} \\
&= \frac{1}{\Pr(T \ge t)} \cd \lim_{\change \downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \change)}{\change}
&& \text{(} \Pr(T \ge t) \text{ does not depend on } \change \text{)} \\
&= \frac{f(t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(density as a limit; } f \text{ is continuous at } t \text{)} \\
&= \frac{f(t)}{\surv(t)}
&& \text{(} \Pr(T = t) = 0 \text{ for continuous } T \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-exp-haz}
#### Hazard function of an exponential distribution

Continuing @exm-exp-survfn,
for $t > 0$, where $f$ is continuous:

$$
\ba
\haz(t)
&= \frac{f(t)}{\surv(t)}
&& \text{(hazard equals density over survival)} \\
&= \frac{\rate \ef{-\rate t}}{\ef{-\rate t}}
&& \text{(substitute the exponential density and survival function)} \\
&= \rate
&& \text{(cancel } \ef{-\rate t} \text{)}
\ea
$$

At $t = 0$, where $f$ jumps from $0$ to $\rate$,
@def-hazard gives the same value directly:
$\Pr(0 \le T < \change \mid T \ge 0) / \change = \paren{1 - \ef{-\rate \change}} / \change \to \rate$
as $\change \downarrow 0$.
So the exponential distribution has a constant hazard for $t \ge 0$,
equal to its rate parameter;
for $t < 0$, $f(t) = 0$, so $\haz(t) = 0$.

:::
